title: The Day the School Stopped Printing Everything
passage:
For years, teachers at Asahi School printed nearly every notice sent to students. Event schedules, club information, homework reminders, and changes to school rules were copied for every class. The system was familiar, but paper use was high, and students often carried home sheets they never read. The school decided to move most notices online.

The first month went badly. Teachers uploaded documents to the school website, but students complained that important information was harder to find. A paper notice had appeared directly on a desk. Online information could be hidden among many files. Some families also shared one device, and younger students sometimes forgot to check the site. Paper use fell, yet missed information increased.

The school realized it had treated ‘digital’ as a delivery method without redesigning how messages were organized. A working group separated notices into three categories. Urgent items, such as a change in tomorrow's schedule, appeared at the top of the student page and triggered a short notification. Weekly information was collected into one summary every Friday. Long-term reference documents, such as club rules, remained in a clearly labeled archive.

Teachers were asked not to send a separate notification for every minor update. During the first digital month, some students had received so many alerts that they stopped paying attention. The new system treated attention as a limited resource. Only information requiring near-term action produced an alert.

The school also kept paper for specific situations. Forms requiring a signature were printed when families requested them. A one-page monthly calendar was available at the office. Students who had difficulty accessing the website could choose a printed weekly summary without having to explain why. The goal changed from ‘eliminate paper’ to ‘use each format where it works best.’

After one term, paper use was about sixty percent lower than before, while reports of missed schedule changes also fell. Teachers spent less time distributing sheets, though they spent more time deciding how to classify information. Most felt the extra thought was useful because notices became shorter and clearer.

The experience taught the school that replacing paper with screens is not automatically modernization. A poor information system remains poor when moved online. In some ways, paper had hidden weaknesses because physical sheets forced information into students' hands. Once that physical reminder disappeared, organization became more important. The successful change came not from choosing digital over paper, but from asking what kind of message was being sent, how quickly people needed it, and what would help them notice it without overwhelming them.
translation:
朝日中学校では長年、行事予定、部活連絡、宿題の注意、校則変更など、ほぼすべての連絡を紙で全員に配っていました。慣れた方法でしたが紙の使用量が多く、読まれないまま持ち帰られることもありました。そこで多くの連絡をオンラインへ移すことにしました。

最初の一か月はうまくいきませんでした。ウェブサイトへ資料を載せても、重要な情報が見つけにくいという不満が出ました。紙なら机の上に直接置かれますが、オンラインでは多数のファイルに埋もれます。端末を家族で共有する家庭や、確認を忘れる生徒もいました。紙は減ったのに、連絡漏れは増えました。

学校は『紙をデジタルに置き換える』だけで、情報整理を設計し直していなかったと気づきました。そこで連絡を三種類に分けました。明日の予定変更など緊急事項はページ上部に表示し短い通知を出す。一週間分の一般情報は金曜にまとめる。部活規則など長期資料は分かりやすい保管場所へ置く、という方法です。

また小さな更新ごとに通知しないようにしました。最初の月は通知が多すぎて無視され始めていたからです。注意力も限られた資源だと考え、近いうちに行動が必要な情報だけ通知しました。

紙も完全にはなくしませんでした。署名が必要な書類は希望に応じて印刷し、月間予定表も窓口で入手できます。ウェブ利用が難しい生徒は理由を説明せず週報の紙版を選べます。目的は『紙ゼロ』ではなく『形式ごとの得意な場面を使う』ことへ変わりました。

一学期後、紙使用量は約六割減り、予定変更の見落とし報告も減りました。教師は配布時間を減らせましたが、情報分類を考える時間は増えました。それでも連絡が短く明確になったため、多くは価値があると感じました。

この経験から、紙を画面へ置き換えるだけでは近代化にならないと分かりました。悪い情報設計はオンラインでも悪いままです。紙は物理的に手元へ届くため、整理の弱さを隠していました。それがなくなると、何の情報か、いつ必要か、どうすれば過剰な通知なしに気づけるかを考えることがより重要になったのです。
